title: Chapter 6 Circular Motion (part 1)
textbookText: Think of circular motion as the result of a balance between two forces–one centrifugal, the other centripetal (toward the center)–rather than as the result of one force, a centripetal force, which constantly deflects the body away from its inertial path in a straight line. Newton extended the dynamics of intermittent colliding bodies to his analysis of bodies subject to a continuous force. He determined the nature of the force directed toward the center of a circle that will move the body uniformly around the circle (i.e., the solution to the direct problem of uniform circular motion). In this analysis, the circular path is approximated by a polygonal path of n sides, where the number of sides of the polygon will ultimately increase without limit. As the number of sides of the polygon was increased, the polygonal path approached a circular path.

6.1 Introduction to Circular Motion Let's engage in the activity to gain an understanding of circular motion: Activity 6.1 i) Take a ball or a stone weighing approximately 100 grams and tie it with an inextensible string. ii) Hold one end of the rope and allow it to move in a circular path. iii) Try to identify the force on the stone and the rope separately with the help of your teacher. iv) Guess the velocity if the rope breaks at A, B, C and D as indicated in the figure. v) Find the change in velocity of the ball between the points A and B, A and C and C and D if |VA| = |VB| = |VC| = |VD| = 5ms-1.

A body is said to be in a circular motion if it remains at an equidistance from a fixed point. This fixed point is called the center of the circular path, and the distance is known as the radius vector. In circular motion, there is a change in velocity at every point along the path. The velocity at each point is given by the tangent drawn at that point. One writes, Velocity = magnitude + direction = speed + direction. At each point, there is a change in the direction of the motion. Therefore, the change in velocity is due to the change in direction. Since there is a change in velocity, acceleration is present, and thus any object undergoing circular motion experiences a force. The force directed towards the center is called the centripetal force, while the force directed away from the center is sometimes referred to as the centrifugal force. However, it's important to note that centrifugal force is more accurately described as a pseudo-force resulting from the inertia of the object. Both forces have equal magnitudes but are directed oppositely. A body moving at a constant speed in circular motion has no net work done on it.

Examples: i) If you whirl a bucket with some water in it in a vertical circle, the water doesn’t fall down due to the centrifugal force that pushes it away from the centre, which is balanced by the inwards centripetal force. ii) While travelling in a bus we lean outwards when the bus undergoes a circular path due to the centrifugal force that finally is balanced by the inwards centripetal force. iii) When a small piece of stone tied to a string is whirled in a circular path, the stone tries to go away by detaching the string due to the action of the centrifugal force and the string is pulling the stone towards the centre due to the centripetal force. iv) Mud flying off a tire is an example of centrifugal force, while a satellite orbiting the Earth is an example of centripetal force.
